title: Iron, Timber, and Names
subtitle: Vardic society and visual identity
summary: Dark iron, wool and knotwork; raven prows and drydocks; and why almost nothing made in the Holds is anonymous.
content:
> *"A machine with no mark is a machine nobody stands behind."*
> — said in Vardic shipyards

You can usually tell something is Vardic before you see the mark on it. Northern work is heavy, practical and built for cold and wet, and it is almost never anonymous. Someone made it, and they want you to know who.

This entry describes how the [Vardic Holds](factions.html#vardic-holds) look: their materials, their ports, their clothing, and the marks and names they put on everything. For why those marks matter so much, see [[old-gods-of-the-holds|The Old Gods of the Holds]]. For how an old seafaring culture became an industrial one, see [[the-vardic-holds|The Vardic Holds]].

## Iron, Timber, Wool and Leather

The Vardic palette is the colour of its materials: **dark iron**, **timber**, **wool** and **leather**, with deep blue, cream and a strong red used for banners, trim and the colours of a Hold. The most common decorative motifs are **knotwork**, **wings**, **anchors** and **diamonds**, and old animal shapes, the raven above all, still appear on prows, clasps and machinery.

![The flag of the Vardic Holds](data/images/vardic-holds-flag-0322b0bc.jpg "The Vardic flag: a raven with spread wings over an anchor, on deep blue, between borders of cream knotwork set with red diamonds. The same motifs recur on clasps, banners and ship prows across the north.")

Vardic design is **functional first**. Ornament is welcome, but it is added to something that already works, and it is rarely allowed to get in the way. A Vardic engine may carry engraved knotwork on its housing; it will not carry a decorative panel that makes it harder to repair. Ceremonial objects are the exception: the regalia of a jarl, a diplomat's crest or a ship launched for a great Hold can be lavish, and everyone understands the difference.

## Ports, Halls and Drydocks

A Vardic port is built where the mountains meet the water. Long timber halls with steep roofs and knotwork banners stand beside foundries, smokestacks and iron cranes. Rail lines run along the quays to the drydocks. Carved standing stones, some far older than the industry around them, still mark harbour entrances.

![A Vardic port in a northern fjord](data/images/vardic-holds-homeland-83dbd42f.jpg "A Hold's industrial harbour. Notice how old and new sit together: long, low iron ships with raven prows in the line of the Hrafneld, cranes and smokestacks above steep-roofed timber halls, and a carved standing stone watching over the water.")

The ships themselves are the clearest signature of the north. Since the *Hrafneld*, Vardic warships and many merchant vessels have kept the **long, low hull**, the carved or cast prow, and engineering that is left visible rather than hidden.

## Maker's Marks

Almost everything made in the Holds carries a **maker's mark**: a small stamped, engraved or cast symbol identifying who made it, and often which workshop, family or Hold they belong to. Marks began on weapons and ships. They moved onto engines, firearms, tools, boilers and entire factories during the Furnace Century.

A mark is not a brand. It is closer to a signature on a promise.

> **A shipwright explains, to an apprentice from abroad**
>
> "You see this? That's my mark. Same as my mother's, with one stroke added so people know it's mine and not hers."
>
> "And if the hull fails?"
>
> "Then everyone who looks at the wreck knows exactly whose fault it was. That's the point, boy. You don't put a mark on work you'd be ashamed to have found."

Pouches, belts and tool rolls often carry their owner's mark too, and many Vards carry small **maker's tokens**: stamped metal pieces they give as proof of work, or as a promise.

## Names

Particularly important machines receive **proper names**, just as ships always have. A famous engine, a foundry's great press or a long-serving locomotive may be known by name across a whole Hold, and its builders are remembered alongside it.

> **A foreign buyer, a Vardic engineering house, and a pumping engine**
>
> "The contract says 'one pumping engine'. Your invoice says *Grim Old Halla*."
>
> "That's her name."
>
> "It's a pump."
>
> "It's a pump that's going to run for forty years without stopping. She's earned a name. If you'd rather she didn't have one, we can build you a different pump." A pause. "It won't be as good."

## What the Vards Wear

The north is cold and wet, and Vardic clothing is built for it: heavy layered **wool**, reinforced **leather**, fur at the collar and hood, sturdy boots, and personalised metal fittings. Clothing announces what someone does. Knotwork and Hold colours on a coat, a crest at the shoulder and the quality of the metalwork mark rank and office.

![Vardic clothing: commoner, diplomat, soldier and Expeditioner](data/images/vardic-holds-clothing-6e438b13.jpg "Four Vards. A harbour worker in durable wool and leather with tools, knives and maker's tokens at the belt; a diplomat whose fur-lined cloak, knotwork and Holds crest show rank and office; a soldier layered against cold and wet in mail, brigandine and iron, Hold colours on the surcoat; and an Expeditioner built for long journeys beyond the Holds, carrying tools, maps, survey gear and prototypes.")

- **Workers** dress for the harbour and the foundry: aprons, heavy gloves, tools in reach, and almost always a maker's token or two.
- **Officials and diplomats** wear fur-lined cloaks and long coats with embroidered knotwork trim. A good brooch or cloak clasp is a statement.
- **Soldiers** wear layered protection for cold, wet conditions, with the colours and knotwork of their Hold on surcoat and gear.
- **Expeditioners** combine all three: practical layers, gear covered in pouches, and equipment marked with their own name or mark.

## Earning a Name

Some Vards carry an accomplishment as part of how they are introduced, as with *Yrsa Halvardsdottir, Builder of the Skeld Turbines* (see [[the-vardic-holds|The Vardic Holds]]). These epithets are given by others, never claimed, and they are meant to be earned.

> **At the Third Dock, after a hard winter**
>
> The chief engineer read out the year's work as she always did, one name at a time. When she reached the youngest engineer on the dock, she stopped.
>
> "Kari Brenn. Kept the number-two crane running through the whole ice season with parts she made herself, because the parts we ordered never came." She let the pause stretch. "From now on, if anyone asks, she's *Kari Brenn, Who Kept the Crane*."
>
> Kari went red to the ears. Someone at the back started banging a wrench on a railing, and the rest of the dock joined in.

## What Foreigners Get Wrong

The most common foreign stereotype of the Vards is the loud northern barbarian: big, blunt and fond of axes. Most Vards find it more tiresome than offensive. Vardic speech *is* direct, and Vardic humour is dry, but the culture that produced the Hrafneld and the Skeld Turbines is precise, patient and deeply technical.

Vards tend to judge a stranger by three questions: what have you done, does your work hold up, and do you keep your word? A visitor who can answer those well will find the Holds far warmer than the climate.
